subject: biology-hl
about: Original practice questions written for NevaIB from the IB guide's syllabus understandings and the school's unit order. Not IB past-paper questions, not publisher material and not IB markschemes: the marking points are written for self-marking. Organisms, experiments and data in data-response items are invented for practice.

items.stem: Amino acids are joined in a polypeptide by:
choices: Peptide bonds formed in condensation reactions
Glycosidic bonds formed in hydrolysis reactions
Hydrogen bonds formed between R groups
Ester bonds formed in condensation reactions
items.note: The amine of one amino acid and the carboxyl of the next react, releasing water.

items.stem: Which part of an amino acid differs between the twenty types?
choices: The amine group
The carboxyl group
The R group (side chain)
The central carbon atom
items.note: All share the same backbone (amine, carboxyl, central C with H). The R group gives each its properties.

items.stem: Essential amino acids are those that:
choices: Are found in every protein of the body
Cannot be made by the body and must be in the diet
Are needed only during growth in children
Are made in the liver from other amino acids whenever the diet lacks them
items.note: Non-essential amino acids can be synthesised from others; essential ones must be eaten.

items.stem: How many different tripeptides can be made from the 20 amino acids?
items.note: 20³ = 8000. Each position can be any of 20 amino acids.

items.stem: A protein is denatured by high temperature. This means that:
choices: Its three-dimensional shape is changed because bonds that hold it are broken
Its amino acid sequence is changed because heat breaks the peptide bonds between neighbouring residues
It is broken down into its separate amino acids
It is converted into a carbohydrate molecule
items.note: Denaturation breaks hydrogen, ionic and other bonds of the 3D structure; peptide bonds remain intact.

items.stem: Extreme pH denatures proteins mainly by:
choices: Breaking the peptide bonds of the primary structure so the chain splits into short fragments
Adding extra amino acids to the polypeptide chain
Removing all water molecules from the protein
Changing the charges on R groups, disrupting ionic and hydrogen bonds
items.note: Added H⁺ or OH⁻ alter the ionisation of R groups, changing the interactions that hold the shape.

items.stem: A diet lacking one essential amino acid would most directly limit:
choices: Synthesis of all carbohydrates in the body
The absorption of fats from the gut
Synthesis of proteins that contain that amino acid
The production of ATP in mitochondria
items.note: Ribosomes need every amino acid in the sequence; missing one stops synthesis of proteins containing it.

items.stem: The primary structure of a protein is:
choices: The coiling of the chain into an α-helix
The sequence of amino acids in the polypeptide
The overall three-dimensional folded shape
The arrangement of several polypeptides together
items.note: Primary = sequence; secondary = α-helix/β-pleated sheet (backbone H-bonds); tertiary = 3D fold; quaternary = several chains.

items.stem: Which bond is involved in secondary but not tertiary structure stabilisation?
choices: Disulfide bonds formed between the R groups of two cysteines far apart in the chain
Ionic bonds between charged R groups
Hydrophobic interactions between non-polar R groups
Hydrogen bonds between C=O and N–H groups of the backbone
items.note: Secondary structure comes from regular backbone hydrogen bonding. Tertiary structure depends on R-group interactions.

items.stem: Haemoglobin is described as a conjugated protein with quaternary structure because it:
choices: Has four polypeptide chains plus non-polypeptide haem groups
Has one polypeptide chain folded into a globular shape
Is made of fibres that give strength
Contains only amino acids and nothing else
items.note: Four subunits (2 α, 2 β) each with a haem group (prosthetic group).

items.stem: Collagen differs from insulin because collagen is:
choices: Globular, with a compact shape and a binding site
Soluble in blood plasma and acts as a hormone
Fibrous, with long parallel chains giving tensile strength
Made of a single short polypeptide chain
items.note: Fibrous proteins are insoluble and structural (collagen, keratin). Globular proteins (insulin, enzymes) are soluble and functional.

items.stem: Outline how a peptide bond is formed between two amino acids.
markscheme: Between the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amine group of the other (1)
A molecule of water is released and a C–N (peptide) bond forms (1)
items.tactic: Name the reaction type, the groups involved and the product released.

items.stem: Explain why proteins can have a very wide range of structures and functions.
markscheme: Twenty different amino acids, with different R groups (1)
Can be joined in any sequence and chain length (1)
Different sequences fold into different 3D shapes, determining function (1)
items.tactic: Diversity explanations: number of building blocks, sequence, shape.

items.stem: Explain how the R groups of amino acids determine the tertiary structure of a protein.
markscheme: Hydrophobic R groups cluster inside, away from water (1)
Ionic bonds between positively and negatively charged R groups (1)
Hydrogen bonds between polar R groups (1)
Disulfide (covalent) bonds between cysteine R groups (1)
Together these determine the specific 3D shape (1)
items.tactic: Name each bond type and say which R groups form it.

items.stem:
(Invented data for practice.) An enzyme extract was kept at different temperatures for 10 minutes, then tested at 30 °C. Activity remaining (%): 30 °C 100; 45 °C 96; 55 °C 60; 65 °C 12; 75 °C 0.
(a) Describe the pattern. (b) Explain the result at 75 °C. (c) Explain why the activity was tested at 30 °C after the heat treatment.
markscheme: (a) Little loss up to 45 °C (96%); sharp fall above 45 °C to 0% at 75 °C (1)
(b) The enzyme was denatured: bonds holding the 3D shape broke and the active site changed permanently (1)
(c) To measure only the permanent effect of heating (denaturation) (1)
and keep the temperature of the assay constant as a controlled variable (1)
items.tactic: Unfamiliar context: find the syllabus idea being tested, quote the data (with units) when you describe a trend, then explain it with that idea. One marking point per linked step.
